note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
tiles.details: Published culms are roughly 15–88 cm and freely branched. Existing panels show long spreading awns and open flowering stems, but no panel proves a rooted annual base. Three awns alone establish Aristida, not A. oligantha.
tiles.short: Wiry annual with an open, few-spikeleted 5–14 cm panicle
tiles.status: VISIBLE FLOWERING HABIT; ROOTED ANNUAL PHOTO GAP

tiles.heading: 02 · TRACE THE ROOTED ANNUAL
tiles.details: Follow one intact flowering culm down to the roots and photograph its branched stem and base together. The archived stem/junction panel is not a root-crown image; a loose panicle cannot establish life history.
tiles.short: Fibrous annual base, not a persistent perennial crown

tiles.heading: 03 · EXPOSE THE TRUE LIGULE
tiles.details: Open the actual blade–sheath junction under 20–40× with a 0.5–1 mm scale. Kew describes a hair-fringe ligule about 0.5 mm; hairs on the sheath or stem junction are not the ligule. No existing panel proves this measurement.
tiles.short: Approximately 0.5 mm fringe of hairs at the inner collar

tiles.heading: 04 · MEASURE BOTH GLUMES
tiles.details: On ONE mature spikelet separate the nearly equal lower and upper glumes. Backlight the lower to count 3–7 veins; upper is typically one-veined and may carry its own 10–15 mm awn. These are Kew treatment ranges, not measurements from the historical drawing in panel 3.
tiles.short: Both about 18–25 mm; lower glume usually 3–7-veined
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — SAME-SPIKELET GLUME PAIR AND LOWER VEINS

tiles.heading: 05 · FOLLOW THREE LEMMA AWNS
tiles.details: One fertile floret bears a three-veined lemma with THREE long, often subequal awn branches from that lemma. The separate upper-glume awn is not a fourth lemma awn. Existing panels 1 and 5 show gross long-awn architecture, not a measured same-lemma insertion or ~1 mm hairy callus.
tiles.short: Fertile lemma 16–28 mm; three spreading awn limbs 30–70 mm
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — DISSECTED LEMMA, AWN FORK AND CALLUS

tiles.heading: 06 · SPLIT FROM PURPLE THREEAWN
tiles.details: Panel 6 is explicitly OTHER SPECIES: A. purpurea. Purple threeawn commonly has a perennial tuft, a one-veined lower glume shorter than its upper; varieties can overlap in upper-glume length. Compare rooted bases and measured paired glumes, never panicle color or three awns alone.
tiles.short: Oldfield annual with long nearly equal glumes; purple perennial
tiles.status: LOOK-ALIKE KEY PRESENT; MATCHED SPECIMEN MACROS MISSING

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: OLD FIELD THREEAWN (native ANNUAL): look for open, few-spikeleted, wiry BRANCHED panicles with three long awns from one lemma. Then inspect ONE mature intact spikelet: lower and upper GLUMES nearly EQUAL in length (~18–25 mm each, awns excluded), lower glume usually 3–7-VEINED. Purple threeawn is perennial with unequal glumes (lower about half upper), generally one lower-glume vein. Panicle shape and color alone cannot decide.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: START with the locally stored field and awn photographs, especially the long thin awns against an open panicle. Three spreading awns suggest Aristida, not oligantha by themselves.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Open the actual blade–sheath junction under 20–40× with a 0.5–1 mm scale. Kew describes a hair-fringe ligule about 0.5 mm; hairs on the sheath or stem junction are not the ligule. No existing panel proves this measurement.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: On ONE mature spikelet separate the nearly equal lower and upper glumes. Backlight the lower to count 3–7 veins; upper is typically one-veined and may carry its own 10–15 mm awn. These are Kew treatment ranges, not measurements from the historical drawing in panel 3.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Use glume relative length and LOWER glume vein count on a mature intact spikelet: A. purpurea has ~6–8 mm lower and ~11–15 mm upper (1-veined lower), while A. oligantha has ~18–25 mm subequal glumes (3–7-veined lower). Confirm a perennial vs annual basal crown; panicle shape and awn color are supporting only.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

intro: OLD FIELD THREEAWN (native ANNUAL): look for open, few-spikeleted, wiry BRANCHED panicles with three long awns from one lemma. Then inspect ONE mature intact spikelet: lower and upper GLUMES nearly EQUAL in length (~18–25 mm each, awns excluded), lower glume usually 3–7-VEINED. Purple threeawn is perennial with unequal glumes (lower about half upper), generally one lower-glume vein. Panicle shape and color alone cannot decide.
memory_rule: OLD FIELD = ANNUAL + long EQUAL glumes and 3–7 lower veins. PURPLE = PERENNIAL + lower glume about HALF upper and one vein.
safety_note: 5 actually photographed local exact-species JPEGs plus 1 public-domain drawing; only photographed anatomical structures count as evidence. USGS flowering awn panel remains externally linked, its server previously timed out. New gallery relink reuses the established locally stored different-species purple-threeawn image; no new oldfield macro or speculative arrow. True glume nerves, precise mm ratio, collar and perennial/annual base are still not documented in a single verified specimen.
field_rule: Three awns alone = genus. Species requires matched lower/upper glume ratio, lower vein count and rooted-life-cycle evidence.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
